claim: The auditory brain contains neurons that decrease their response to repetitive sounds but increase their firing rate to novel or deviant stimuli.
source: The auditory brain contains neurons that decrease their response to repetitive sounds but increase their firing rate to novel or deviant stimuli; the difference between both responses is known as stimulus-specific adaptation or neuronal mismatch (nMM).
evidence: This is a well-established finding in auditory neuroscience, supported by the broader literature context.

claim: The difference between responses to repetitive and novel stimuli is known as stimulus-specific adaptation or neuronal mismatch (nMM).
source: The auditory brain contains neurons that decrease their response to repetitive sounds but increase their firing rate to novel or deviant stimuli; the difference between both responses is known as stimulus-specific adaptation or neuronal mismatch (nMM).
evidence: This is a definition provided in the manuscript.

claim: ACh modulates the nMM, affecting prediction error responses but not repetition suppression.
source: Results indicate that ACh modulates the nMM, affecting prediction error responses but not repetition suppression, and this effect is manifested predominantly in infragranular cortical layers.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly shown in Figure 7.

claim: The effect of ACh on nMM is manifested predominantly in infragranular cortical layers.
source: Results indicate that ACh modulates the nMM, affecting prediction error responses but not repetition suppression, and this effect is manifested predominantly in infragranular cortical layers.
evidence: This is supported by the depth analysis shown in Figure 8 and Figure 10.

claim: The differential effect of ACh on responses to standards, relative to deviants, was consistent with representational sharpening that accompanies an increase in the precision of prediction errors.
source: The differential effect of ACh on responses to standards, relative to deviants (in terms of averages and variances), was consistent with the representational sharpening that accompanies an increase in the precision of prediction errors.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on predictive coding theory, supported by the variance analysis in Figure 8.

claim: ACh plays an important role in modulating prediction error signaling in the AC.
source: These findings suggest that ACh plays an important role in modulating prediction error signaling in the AC and gating the access of these signals to higher cognitive levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings, particularly the effects on iPE shown in Figure 7.

claim: ACh gates the access of prediction error signals to higher cognitive levels.
source: These findings suggest that ACh plays an important role in modulating prediction error signaling in the AC and gating the access of these signals to higher cognitive levels.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental findings and predictive coding framework.

claim: Acetylcholine (ACh) is a widely distributed neuromodulator throughout the brain, including the AC.
source: Acetylcholine (ACh) is a widely distributed neuromodulator throughout the brain, including the AC, and modulates processes such as attention, learning, memory, arousal, sleep, and/or cognitive reinforcement (Batista-Brito et al., 2018; Dalley et al., 2004; Franklin and Frank, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ACh modulates processes such as attention, learning, memory, arousal, sleep, and/or cognitive reinforcement.
source: Acetylcholine (ACh) is a widely distributed neuromodulator throughout the brain, including the AC, and modulates processes such as attention, learning, memory, arousal, sleep, and/or cognitive reinforcement (Batista-Brito et al., 2018; Dalley et al., 2004; Franklin and Frank, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The main source of ACh to the AC is the basal forebrain.
source: The main source of ACh to the AC is the basal forebrain (Chavez and Zaborszky, 2017; Mesulam, 2013; Zaborszky et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cholinergic modulation alters frequency response areas generating changes across frequency tuning, decreasing the acoustic threshold at the characteristic frequency, and changing the encoding of the spectral representation of many auditory neurons.
source: In the auditory system, cholinergic modulation is known to alter frequency response areas generating changes across frequency tuning, decreasing the acoustic threshold at the characteristic frequency, and changing the encoding of the spectral representation of many auditory neurons (Ma and Suga, 2005; Metherate, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ACh promotes neuronal and synaptic plasticity at different temporal scales.
source: Thus, ACh promotes neuronal and synaptic plasticity at different temporal scales (Kamke et al., 2005; Kilgard and Merzenich, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SSA is elicited by an oddball paradigm, which comprises a pattern of repeating sounds (standards), interrupted by a low-probability and unexpected sound (deviant).
source: SSA is elicited by an oddball paradigm, which comprises a pattern of repeating sounds (standards), interrupted by a low-probability and unexpected sound (deviant).
evidence: This is a methodological description of the experimental paradigm.

claim: The deviant usually differs in frequency, but could differ on any other physical dimension from the standard sound, or otherwise violate a pattern of regularity established by the standard.
source: The deviant usually differs in frequency, but could differ on any other physical dimension from the standard sound, or otherwise violate a pattern of regularity established by the standard (Chen et al., 2015; Nieto-Diego and Malmierca, 2016; Parras et al., 2017; Ulanovsky et al., 2003; von der Behrens et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Neurons that exhibit SSA adapt specifically to the standard stimulus but resume their firing when a deviant stimulus appears.
source: Thus, neurons that exhibit SSA adapt specifically to the standard stimulus but resume their firing when a deviant stimulus appears.
evidence: This is a description of the SSA phenomenon based on established knowledge.

claim: SSA has been proposed to be a neuronal correlate of 'mismatch negativity (MMN)', an evoked potential obtained in human and animal electroencephalographic studies using the oddball paradigm.
source: SSA has been proposed to be a neuronal correlate of 'mismatch negativity (MMN)', an evoked potential obtained in human and animal electroencephalographic studies using the oddball paradigm (Nieto-Diego and Malmierca, 2016; Ulanovsky et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: nMM is considered a form of short-term plasticity.
source: Because nMM is considered a form of short-term plasticity (Ogawa and Oka, 2015) and ACh has been shown to play a role in this type of neural plasticity (Marshall et al., 2016; Moran et al., 2013; Parr and Friston, 2017; Vossel et al., 2012) it is plausible that ACh may be involved in the generation and/or modulation of nMM.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: ACh has been shown to play a role in short-term plasticity.
source: Because nMM is considered a form of short-term plasticity (Ogawa and Oka, 2015) and ACh has been shown to play a role in this type of neural plasticity (Marshall et al., 2016; Moran et al., 2013; Parr and Friston, 2017; Vossel et al., 2012) it is plausible that ACh may be involved in the generation and/or modulation of nMM.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: ACh differentially modulates the neural response to the standard stimulus in neurons of the IC.
source: Furthermore, it has been shown that ACh differentially modulates the neural response to the standard stimulus in neurons of the IC (Ayala and Malmierca, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: MMN and nMM are best explained by the predictive coding theory.
source: Currently, MMN and nMM are best explained by the predictive coding theory (Friston and Sporns, 2008; Friston, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: According to the predictive coding framework, higher-level cortical areas generate predictions about sensory streams that are conveyed in a top-down manner to lower hierarchical levels, to suppress the ascending neuronal activity evoked by sensory events that can be anticipated.
source: According to the predictive coding framework, higher-level cortical areas generate predictions about sensory streams that are conveyed in a top-down manner to lower hierarchical levels, to suppress the ascending neuronal activity evoked by sensory events that can be anticipated.
evidence: This is a description of predictive coding theory.

claim: When current predictions do not match the sensory inputs, the lower levels send forward bottom-up prediction errors to higher hierarchical levels.
source: However, when current predictions do not match the sensory inputs, the lower levels then send forward bottom-up prediction errors to higher hierarchical levels (Friston and Kiebel, 2009).
evidence: This is a description of predictive coding theory, supported by a citation.

claim: In the setting of an oddball paradigm, every evoked response is considered to be a prediction error response.
source: In the setting of an oddball paradigm, every evoked response is considered to be a prediction error response.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on predictive coding theory.

claim: When the stimulus does not change, sensory learning enables better predictions to progressively attenuate the response to standards until an oddball or deviant stimulus is encountered — and a large prediction error is seen.
source: When the stimulus does not change, sensory learning enables better predictions to progressively attenuate the response to standards until an oddball or deviant stimulus is encountered — and a large prediction error is seen.
evidence: This is an explanation based on predictive coding theory.

claim: Predictive coding models weigh sensory prediction errors by their precision, which is the inverse of the variance.
source: The prediction error response to oddball stimuli may be further augmented by increasing the precision or gain of prediction errors: predictive coding models weigh sensory prediction errors by their precision, which is the inverse of the variance.
evidence: This is a description of predictive coding theory.

claim: Precision weighting of prediction errors encodes the confidence in the accuracy of the information in terms of their signal-to-noise ratio.
source: Precision weighting of prediction errors, therefore, encodes the confidence in the accuracy of the information (i.e. prediction errors) in terms of their signal-to-noise ratio (Parr and Friston, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Precision has been suggested to be mediated by synaptic gain modulation.
source: In neurobiological terms, precision has been suggested to be mediated by synaptic gain modulation; namely, the sensitivity of postsynaptic responses to neural inputs (Adams et al., 2022), and is likely implemented by cholinergic neuromodulation (Moran et al., 2013; Yu and Dayan, 2005; Yu and Dayan, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Precision is likely implemented by cholinergic neuromodulation.
source: In neurobiological terms, precision has been suggested to be mediated by synaptic gain modulation; namely, the sensitivity of postsynaptic responses to neural inputs (Adams et al., 2022), and is likely implemented by cholinergic neuromodulation (Moran et al., 2013; Yu and Dayan, 2005; Yu and Dayan, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There are two mechanisms underlying the MMN/nMM according to the predictive coding model.
source: According to the predictive coding model, there are, therefore, two mechanisms underlying the MMN/nMM (Auksztulewicz and Friston, 2016; Carbajal and Malmierca, 2018; Friston and Sporns, 2008; Harms et al., 2021; Parras et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: nMM could reflect the repetition suppression (RS) of the response to the predictable stimuli (standards) due to sensory learning.
source: First, nMM could reflect the repetition suppression (RS) of the response to the predictable stimuli (standards) due to sensory learning – that resolves sensory prediction errors as predictions become more accurate.
evidence: This is an explanation based on predictive coding theory.

claim: nMM could also reflect an increase in the precision or gain afforded prediction errors, when the (oddball) stimulus cannot be predicted.
source: In addition, nMM could also reflect an increase in the precision or gain afforded prediction errors, when the (oddball) stimulus cannot be predicted; enabling the ascending prediction errors to revise higher-level representations about the auditory stream.
evidence: This is an explanation based on predictive coding theory.

claim: Repetition suppression and prediction error modulation can be distinguished using control sequences.
source: Repetition suppression and prediction error modulation can be distinguished using control sequences (Ruhnau et al., 2012), and there is now evidence in both humans and rodents that MMN/nMM receives contributions from both prediction error (modulation) and repetition suppression (sensory learning) at various levels of the auditory system (Ishishita et al., 2019; Parras et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There is evidence in both humans and rodents that MMN/nMM receives contributions from both prediction error (modulation) and repetition suppression (sensory learning) at various levels of the auditory system.
source: Repetition suppression and prediction error modulation can be distinguished using control sequences (Ruhnau et al., 2012), and there is now evidence in both humans and rodents that MMN/nMM receives contributions from both prediction error (modulation) and repetition suppression (sensory learning) at various levels of the auditory system (Ishishita et al., 2019; Parras et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A total of 113 units were recorded in the AC before, during and after the microiontophoretic injection of acetylcholine in the rat.
source: To explore the influence of cholinergic modulation on nMM, we recorded a total of 113 units in the AC before, during and after the microiontophoretic injection of acetylcholine in the rat.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental sample.

claim: Recording depths ranged from 120–1191 μm including neurons from all layers.
source: Recording depths ranged from 120–1191 μm including neurons from all layers.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental sample.

claim: A high-frequency reversal zone was found between ventral auditory field (VAF, caudally) and anterior auditory field (AAF, rostrally).
source: Similar to these previous studies, we found a high-frequency reversal zone between ventral auditory field (VAF, caudally) and anterior auditory field (AAF, rostrally), a low-frequency reversal zone between A1 and posterior auditory field (PAF, dorso-caudally), and a high-frequency reversal between VAF and supra-rhinal auditory field (SRAF, ventrally).
evidence: This is a description of the tonotopic organization observed in the data, shown in Figure 1.

claim: A low-frequency reversal zone was found between A1 and posterior auditory field (PAF, dorso-caudally).
source: Similar to these previous studies, we found a high-frequency reversal zone between ventral auditory field (VAF, caudally) and anterior auditory field (AAF, rostrally), a low-frequency reversal zone between A1 and posterior auditory field (PAF, dorso-caudally), and a high-frequency reversal between VAF and supra-rhinal auditory field (SRAF, ventrally).
evidence: This is a description of the tonotopic organization observed in the data, shown in Figure 1.

claim: A high-frequency reversal was found between VAF and supra-rhinal auditory field (SRAF, ventrally).
source: Similar to these previous studies, we found a high-frequency reversal zone between ventral auditory field (VAF, caudally) and anterior auditory field (AAF, rostrally), a low-frequency reversal zone between A1 and posterior auditory field (PAF, dorso-caudally), and a high-frequency reversal between VAF and supra-rhinal auditory field (SRAF, ventrally).
evidence: This is a description of the tonotopic organization observed in the data, shown in Figure 1.

claim: On average, the firing rate decreased during the application of ACh (mean control: 5.8±7.0 spikes/s, mean ACh: 4.7±10.3 spikes/s; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p<0.001).
source: On average, the firing rate decreased during the application of ACh (mean control: 5.8±7.0 spikes/s, mean ACh: 4.7±10.3 spikes/s; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: Most neurons recovered their basal firing rates after 60–90 min after the ACh injection (recovery mean: 6.5±8.1 spikes/s, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.4, control vs. recovery).
source: Most neurons recovered their basal firing rates after 60–90 min after the ACh injection (recovery mean: 6.5±8.1 spikes/s, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.4, control vs. recovery).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: No significant changes occur in BW10 (control: 0.76±0.57 octaves; effect: 0.88±0.75 octaves; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.248).
source: Indeed, no significant changes occur in neither BW10 (control: 0.76±0.57 oc taves; effect: 0.88±0.75 oc taves; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.248) nor BW30 (control: 1.33±0.73 oc taves; effect: 1.43±0.80 oc taves; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.664) (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 4.

claim: No significant changes occur in BW30 (control: 1.33±0.73 octaves; effect: 1.43±0.80 octaves; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.664).
source: Indeed, no significant changes occur in neither BW10 (control: 0.76±0.57 oc taves; effect: 0.88±0.75 oc taves; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.248) nor BW30 (control: 1.33±0.73 oc taves; effect: 1.43±0.80 oc taves; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.664) (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 4.

claim: ACh produced a significant increase of the CSI value in 26% (22/85, bootstrapping, 95% c.i.) of the neurons recorded.
source: ACh produced a significant increase of the CSI value in 26% (Figure 5a, purple dots; 22/85, bootstrapping, 95% c.i.) and a significant decrease in 31% of the neurons recorded (Figure 5a, orange dots; 26/85, bootstrapping, 95% c.i.).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 5.

claim: ACh produced a significant decrease of the CSI value in 31% (26/85, bootstrapping, 95% c.i.) of the neurons recorded.
source: ACh produced a significant increase of the CSI value in 26% (Figure 5a, purple dots; 22/85, bootstrapping, 95% c.i.) and a significant decrease in 31% of the neurons recorded (Figure 5a, orange dots; 26/85, bootstrapping, 95% c.i.).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 5.

claim: Thirty-seven units (43%) were unaffected by ACh.
source: Thirty-seven units (43%) were unaffected by ACh.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: The average CSI during ACh injection (CSI = 0.54±0.27) was similar to that of the control condition (CSI = 0.57±0.23; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.359).
source: The average CSI during ACh injection (CSI = 0.54±0.27) was similar to that of the control condition (CSI = 0.57±0.23; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.359; Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 5.

claim: ACh produced a significant decrease in the mean firing rate in response to the deviant tones (11.75±17.46 Hz) as compared to the control condition (16.51±16.19 Hz; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p<0.001).
source: We observed that ACh produced a significant decrease in the mean firing rate in response to the deviant tones (Figure 5c; 11.75±17.46 Hz), as compared to the control condition (16.51±16.19 Hz; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p<0.001), as well as in the mean firing rate in response to standard tones (Figure 5c; 4.58±6.38 vs. 3.97±9.90 Hz, control vs ACh; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 5.

claim: ACh produced a significant decrease in the mean firing rate in response to standard tones (4.58±6.38 vs. 3.97±9.90 Hz, control vs ACh; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.001).
source: We observed that ACh produced a significant decrease in the mean firing rate in response to the deviant tones (Figure 5c; 11.75±17.46 Hz), as compared to the control condition (16.51±16.19 Hz; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p<0.001), as well as in the mean firing rate in response to standard tones (Figure 5c; 4.58±6.38 vs. 3.97±9.90 Hz, control vs ACh; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 5.

claim: The mean AUC decreased significantly during the application of ACh (0.74±0.13 vs. 0.67±0.15, control vs. effect; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p<0.001).
source: This analysis shows that the mean AUC decreased significantly during the application of ACh (0.74±0.13 vs. 0.67±0.15, control vs. effect; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 5.

claim: Mutual Information decreased significantly during the application of ACh (0.09±0.07 vs. 0.07±0.08, control vs. effect; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.003).
source: The same happened for Mutual Information (Figure 5d, right panel; 0.09±0.07 vs. 0.07±0.08, control vs. effect; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.003).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 5.

claim: Under the influence of ACh, neurons are less able to discriminate deviant stimuli from standard stimuli.
source: These AUC and Mutual Information analyses indicate that under the influence of ACh, neurons are less able to discriminate deviant stimuli from standard stimuli.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the AUC and Mutual Information results.

claim: ACh produced a significant increase of the SI in 27% of the frequencies recorded (55/205, bootstrapping, 95% c.i.).
source: This analysis shows that ACh produced a significant increase of the SI in 27% of the frequencies recorded (Figure 6a, purple dots; 55/205, bootstrapping, 95% c.i.), 31% (64/205; Figure 6a, orange dots) showed a significant decrease of their SI and 42% frequencies (86/205) were unaffected by ACh.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 6.

claim: 31% (64/205) of frequencies showed a significant decrease of their SI.
source: This analysis shows that ACh produced a significant increase of the SI in 27% of the frequencies recorded (Figure 6a, purple dots; 55/205, bootstrapping, 95% c.i.), 31% (64/205; Figure 6a, orange dots) showed a significant decrease of their SI and 42% frequencies (86/205) were unaffected by ACh.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 6.

claim: 42% frequencies (86/205) were unaffected by ACh.
source: This analysis shows that ACh produced a significant increase of the SI in 27% of the frequencies recorded (Figure 6a, purple dots; 55/205, bootstrapping, 95% c.i.), 31% (64/205; Figure 6a, orange dots) showed a significant decrease of their SI and 42% frequencies (86/205) were unaffected by ACh.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 6.

claim: The mean SI (SI = 0.55±0.31, control condition) was reduced during ACh injection (SI = 0.40±0.50) although this decrease was not significant (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.086).
source: The mean SI (SI = 0.55±0.31, control condition) was reduced during ACh injection (SI = 0.40±0.50) although this decrease was not significant (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.086; Figure 6b).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 6.

claim: In frequencies showing SI decrease, the effect of ACh was significantly different for the deviant- and standard stimuli (p<0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
source: In frequencies showing SI decrease, the effect of ACh was significantly different for the deviant- and standard stimuli (Figure 6c, top panel; p<0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 6.

claim: In frequencies showing SI decrease, the firing rate change ratio was clearly negative for deviant sounds (p<0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test) and not significant for standards (p=0.256, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
source: Furthermore, this ratio was clearly negative for deviant sounds (p<0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test) and not significant for standards (p=0.256, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), indicating that ACh caused a reduction of the firing rate differentially during deviant stimuli.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 6.

claim: In frequencies showing SI increase, the effect of ACh had a distinct effect on the deviant- and standard stimuli (p<0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
source: On the other hand, in frequencies showing SI increase the effect of ACh also had a distinct effect on the deviant- and standard stimuli (Figure 6d, top panel; p<0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), but in this case, the effects were reverse: the change ratio was clearly negative for standard sounds (p=0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test) and not significant for deviant ones (p=0.379, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), hence ACh caused a reduction of the firing rate primarily during standard stimuli.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 6.

claim: In frequencies showing SI increase, the change ratio was clearly negative for standard sounds (p=0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test) and not significant for deviant ones (p=0.379, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
source: On the other hand, in frequencies showing SI increase the effect of ACh also had a distinct effect on the deviant- and standard stimuli (Figure 6d, top panel; p<0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), but in this case, the effects were reverse: the change ratio was clearly negative for standard sounds (p=0.001, Wilcoxon signed-rank test) and not significant for deviant ones (p=0.379, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), hence ACh caused a reduction of the firing rate primarily during standard stimuli.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 6.

claim: In frequencies showing SI decrease, both ROC AUC and Mutual Information decreased significantly during ACh application (p<0.001 in both cases, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
source: In frequencies showing SI decrease (Figure 6c, bottom panel) both ROC AUC and Mutual Information decreased significantly during ACh application (p<0.001 in both cases, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), in line with the results obtained for the whole sample (compare to Figure 5d).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 6.

claim: In frequencies showing SI increase, ROC AUC did not change significantly (p=0.339), while Mutual Information increased slightly (p=0.008).
source: However, in frequencies showing SI increase (Figure 6d, bottom panel) ROC AUC did not change significantly (p=0.339), while Mutual Information increased slightly (p=0.008).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 6.

claim: Frequencies showing SI decrease are the ones mediating the main effects of ACh in the population.
source: These results suggest that frequencies showing SI decrease are the ones mediating the main effects of ACh in the population.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differential effects observed in the data.

claim: ACh led to a significant decrease in the DEV responses in those units where SI decreased (Wilcoxon Signed Rank test, p<0.001).
source: ACh led to a significant decrease in the DEV responses in those units where SI decreased (Figure 7a; Wilcoxon Signed Rank test, p<0.001) and to a significant increase in those units where SI increased (Figure 7b; p=0.011).

claim: ACh led to a significant increase in the DEV responses in those units where SI increased (p=0.011).

claim: ACh caused a decrease in STD responses in units where SI increased (p<0.001).

evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 7.

claim: There were no significant changes in CAS (p=0.091 and p=0.072, for SI decrease and increase, respectively).
source: While this trend is very clear, there were no significant changes in CAS (p=0.091 and p=0.072, for SI decrease and increase, respectively).

source: Significant effects of ACh administration were found for iMM and iPE, both in SI decrease units (iPE: p<0.001; iMM: p<0.001; Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 7c) and SI increase units (iPE: p=0.023; iMM: p<0.001; Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 7d), while iRS remained unchanged (SI decrease units iRS: p=0.121; SI increase units iRS: p=0.675; Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 7.

claim: Significant effects of ACh administration were found for iMM and iPE in SI increase units (iPE: p=0.023; iMM: p<0.001; Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
source: Significant effects of ACh administration were found for iMM and iPE, both in SI decrease units (iPE: p<0.001; iMM: p<0.001; Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 7c) and SI increase units (iPE: p=0.023; iMM: p<0.001; Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 7d), while iRS remained unchanged (SI decrease units iRS: p=0.121; SI increase units iRS: p=0.675; Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 7.

claim: iRS remained unchanged in both SI decrease units (p=0.121) and SI increase units (p=0.675).
source: Significant effects of ACh administration were found for iMM and iPE, both in SI decrease units (iPE: p<0.001; iMM: p<0.001; Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 7c) and SI increase units (iPE: p=0.023; iMM: p<0.001; Wilcoxon signed-rank test; Figure 7d), while iRS remained unchanged (SI decrease units iRS: p=0.121; SI increase units iRS: p=0.675; Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 7.

claim: ACh decreased significantly iMM (0.72±0.13 vs. 0.52±0.36, control vs. effect; p<0.001) and iPE (0.33±0.33 vs. 0.145±0.48, control vs. effect; p=0.004) in high SI frequencies.
